title: the family word he chose
tomorrow: why people stand up when the book comes in

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Hail Mary, a greeting, then a request. Today, the prayer on the single beads between the tens. Day eleven.

A boss gets the best email voice. A judge gets your honor. A king, in the old days, got your majesty, said from the knees. The more powerful someone is, the more careful and formal the words. In Luke's Gospel, a disciple asks Jesus: teach us to pray. How do you talk to the one who made the stars? Titles, you might expect. A long list of them. Instead he gives them a prayer that begins with a family word.
screen: `YOUR HONOR. YOUR MAJESTY.` → `TEACH US TO PRAY.` → `A FAMILY WORD.`

segments.voice: In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, it starts: "Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name." Father. Behind the Greek of the Gospels, some scholars hear the Aramaic word abba. Mark's Gospel keeps that word untranslated, on the night before Jesus died, when he prays in the garden: "Abba, Father, all things are possible to thee." Abba is the word a son or daughter uses. Not a title. A relationship. And then look at the word before it: our. Not my Father. Our. Read it closely and there isn't a single I or me in the whole prayer. Give us. Forgive us. Lead us. Deliver us. Someone praying it alone at night still prays in the plural, standing in a crowd they can't see. That's the family word doing its work twice: God is not a stranger, and neither is the person next to you. At Mass, the whole room prays it together, just before communion. For a long time Catholics prayed it in Latin: Pater noster, our Father. One difference shows up in other churches. Churches that learned the prayer from the King James Bible end with: for thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory. The King James prints that line in Matthew; the Douay-Rheims, translated from the Latin, ends at deliver us from evil, and so do Catholics. At Mass, the priest adds a short prayer after it, and then everyone says a version of that ending together. Same prayer, two old habits.
screen: `ABBA — FATHER, AT HOME.` · `OUR, NOT MY.` · `NO I, NO ME.` · `PATER NOSTER.` · then, large: `NOT A STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Say just the first two words, slowly, out loud or silently: our Father. On our, think of someone you'd rather not include in that word, and include them anyway. On Father, notice how different it sounds from a title. If you pray the whole prayer, you can pray it once, very slowly.
The Our Father. The prayer Jesus taught, opening with a family word, with no I or me in it anywhere. Eleventh word.
Your line: not a stranger. Not God, and not the person beside you. See you tomorrow.

options: with a long list of royal titles.
fork.reveal: "our Father who art in heaven." a family word, in the plural.

original.note: Latin: our Father. the prayer's first two words in Latin, which became its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prayer everyone memorizes as kids.
what it means: a prayer that calls God by a family word and never once says I or me.
what a scholar hears: abba behind the Greek pater; the doxology printed in the King James Matthew but not in the Latin Vulgate; the Mass adding a form of it after the priest's embolism.
